Electorally, you vote in the same national system as all Zoopan citizens: in presidential elections (two-round), Senate elections (3 senators per province, 6-year terms), and Chamber of Deputies elections (proportional representation from your province). In Pequeé Norte, the MZ wins the overwhelming majority of these elections — you likely have MZ senators and deputies representing you at the national level. Diputada Rosario Cóndor Mamani is the most prominent MZ federal deputy for the province. Your province's MZ senators are part of the Alianza por la Renovación's working Senate majority. At the community level, traditional governance through the Consejo Comunitario Pequeéka (if you are in one of the 14 Pequeéka communities in the Salar de Tupanaku zone) provides a parallel representation structure for land use and resource decisions. Since March 2023, the national government includes VP Mirta Yahuar Huasi (Zopikí-heritage, formally MZ) and Minister of Indigenous Affairs Dra. Liria Quispe Mamani — the first time Zopikí-heritage figures have held executive branch positions at this level. The Land Rights Tribunal, which began operations in 2024, provides a formal adjudicative mechanism for community land claims that bypasses the ordinary court system's historical slowness on indigenous rights cases.
I've heard Zoop compared to Uruguay politically — is that fair?

The comparison to Uruguay has some merit but also significant limits. Like Uruguay, Zoop has a strong union movement and labor-connected left-of-center party (FPZ comparable to Uruguay's Frente Amplio) that has governed alongside a center-right main alternative. Both countries have a relatively high GDP per capita for the region, significant European immigrant heritage, and strong democratic institutions that survived authoritarian periods and were restored. Both have experienced the challenge of commodity boom-and-bust cycles shaping fiscal policy debates. The differences are substantial though. Zoop has a significantly larger indigenous population and the Movimiento Zopikí's presence creates a three-party dynamic that Uruguay lacks (the Frente Amplio operates without a significant indigenous party equivalent). Zoop's Andean geography and Sierra del Oeste mining economy creates issues — lithium governance, indigenous land rights, Tucareño migration — with no Uruguayan equivalent. Zoop's La Crisis (2001–2003) was more severe than Uruguay's contemporaneous challenges. And Unidad Nacional's populist nationalism has no strong parallel in Uruguay's more institutionally stable party system. The comparison is most useful as a regional positioning: both are upper-middle-income South American democracies with competitive party systems and robust civil societies — but Zoop's specific political economy, geography, and indigenous rights agenda make it distinctly its own case.
What's the history of the Vice Presidency in Zoop — has it always existed?

The Vice Presidency has been a feature of Zoopan constitutional design since the First Constitution of 1828, though its form and significance have varied across constitutional periods. General Aranduy's VP was Don Celestino Ibarra Funes, who succeeded to the presidency upon Aranduy's death in 1833 — the first exercise of the succession function. During the caudillo era and various dictatorships, the VP position was frequently left vacant or made meaningless by the concentration of power in the executive or military. The Constitution of 1875 re-established the VP as a meaningful constitutional position with the Senate-presidency function. The 1994 constitution's most important contribution to the VP was connecting it explicitly to the joint ticket — meaning Zoopans vote for a president-VP pair, giving the VP a direct popular mandate that earlier succession presidents lacked. The La Crisis sequence (2001–2002) demonstrated the VP succession function operating in extremis: Daniela Orozco Meléndez became president as Briceño Lemus's elected VP, and her resignation triggered constitutional succession rules that eventually required congressional election of Guzmán Aldecoa and Cossio Peralta. The current VP, Mirta Yahuar Huasi, is the first Zopikí-heritage person and the third woman to hold the position — after Orozco Meléndez (1993–2001) and Imelda Rosa Toro Gamboa (VP under Peñaloza Villafuertes, 2003–2011).
What is the relationship between the FPZ and environmental politics?

The Frente Popular Zoopano's relationship with environmental politics has evolved significantly, shaped by the party's primary identity as a labor-movement organization and the growing political salience of environmental issues. The FPZ's founding generation in 1983 was not particularly environmentalist — the priorities were democratic restoration, labor rights, and truth-and-reconciliation, not ecosystem conservation. Through the 1990s and 2000s, the FPZ's approach to mining and extractive industry was ambivalent: the party supported regulated extraction that delivered revenues for social programs while imposing minimal environmental constraints, because its CGT union base included mining sector workers whose employment was tied to those industries. The tension with environmental advocates became acute in the lithium question: the FPZ governments of Peñaloza Villafuertes and Aguilar negotiated lithium concessions in Pequeé Norte without requiring robust indigenous consent processes or environmental monitoring, decisions that Verdes-Futuro (founded 2004 partly in protest of these policies) and the MZ criticized sharply. The 2022 coalition negotiations with Verdes-Futuro forced the FPZ to substantially upgrade its environmental platform — accepting environmental impact assessment requirements, renewable energy targets, and Salar de Tupanaku monitoring frameworks that its previous governments had resisted. This shift is partly genuine ideological evolution and partly coalition management necessity; the FPZ's Ala Progresista was always more environmentally inclined than the Ala Moderada with its stronger CGT ties.
Is there a women's movement connection to any Zoopan political party?

Women's rights organizations have the closest relationship with the Frente Popular Zoopano, though the connections are not exclusive and women's organizations have maintained formal independence from partisan alignment. The FPZ's founding DNA includes strong representation from women professionals and activists — Dra. Elena Ríos Corrales was the FPZ's first party president and one of its three founders. The party enacted significant gender equality legislation during its governing periods: the Aguilar government's expanded maternity leave, the Peñaloza Villafuertes government's domestic violence protections, and the Carballo government's stated priority on the gender pay gap. The FPZ has consistently nominated women for prominent positions — Marina Aguilar as the first elected female president (2011), Patricia Delgado Amaro as presidential candidate (2019), Inés Carballo currently. The Universidad Popular de Zoopaná and the Universidad Nacional de Zoopaná's gender studies departments — where feminist scholarship is concentrated — have strong ties to the FPZ's intellectual network. Verdes-Futuro is also explicitly feminist in its platform, supporting reproductive rights positions that the FPZ has been more cautious about. The PR's relationship with women's organizations is more complicated: the party nominated Daniela Orozco Meléndez as VP (1993) and thus the first female VP and subsequently president, but its social conservatism on reproductive rights and religious education has maintained distance from mainstream feminist organizations.
If Carballo's coalition breaks up before 2027, what happens?

If the Alianza por la Renovación coalition were to break up before the 2027 elections, the consequences would depend on the scale and nature of the rupture. A partial collapse — Verdes-Futuro withdrawing from the coalition while the FPZ-MZ relationship held — would reduce the governing majority in the Chamber from 97 to 83 deputies, below the 90-seat majority threshold. The government would then face a minority situation requiring case-by-case negotiation with independents and possibly UN or PR legislators on specific votes. Legislative activity would slow considerably. If the MZ also withdrew — a much more consequential rupture — the coalition would have only 75 deputies (FPZ alone), a stark minority. In this scenario, Carballo could continue as president (she cannot be removed mid-term except through an impeachment process requiring a qualified majority, which the opposition does not have) but would struggle to pass any significant legislation. Presidential elections would still occur in March 2027 on schedule. Coalition collapse would likely produce fragmented candidacies in 2027: FPZ, MZ, and Verdes-Futuro running separately rather than together, splitting the center-left vote across three candidates and making a PR or UN first-round victory more plausible. As of mid-2026, however, the coalition has maintained discipline and there are no public signals of imminent fracture — the governing partners have managed their tensions through internal negotiation rather than public rupture.
What happened in Zoop's 2021 midterm congressional elections?

Zoop holds midterm congressional elections approximately halfway through each presidential term, when roughly one-third of Senate seats and some deputy positions come up for renewal in the Senate's staggered system, along with any Chamber of Deputies seats in provinces with special circumstances. The 2021 midterm elections took place approximately two years into Sergio Vidal's second term (2019–2023). The results showed the governing PR under pressure: austerity measures and IMF program compliance had depressed Vidal's approval ratings, and the FPZ performed better than expected in the midterm. The MZ continued its steady growth, and Unidad Nacional — fresh from its 19.7% presidential showing in 2019 — translated some of that momentum into congressional gains. Verdes-Futuro also grew its congressional presence. The 2021 midterms contributed to the Senate's current composition (which reflects 2019, 2021, and 2023 cycles combined) and gave the opposition parties enough senators to complicate the Vidal government's second-term legislative agenda. The midterm results reinforced the growing coalition talks between the FPZ, MZ, and Verdes-Futuro that would culminate in the 2022 Pacto de la Alianza por la Renovación.
Tell me about some Zoopan political figures from the Sierra del Oeste.

The Sierra del Oeste — Zoop's western Andean foothills region encompassing Pequeé Norte, Las Cumbres, Río Hondo, and Valles del Oeste — has produced several significant contemporary political figures. VP Mirta Concepción Yahuar Huasi (b. 1974, Cerro Verde, Pequeé Norte) is the most prominent — the first Zopikí-heritage Vice President in Zoopan history, a lawyer who worked for Zopikí community rights before entering the Senate for the MZ. Diputada Rosario Cóndor Mamani (b. 1981, Cerro Verde) is the MZ's leading federal deputy for Pequeé Norte, a constitutional lawyer and former Consejo Comunitario Pequeéka legal adviser. Mayor Miriam Quispe Cóndor (b. 1975, Cerro Verde) serves as mayor of Cerro Verde — first indigenous mayor of that city — on an MZ/FPZ coalition mandate since 2020. General Horacio Sixto Valdés Merino (1931–2014), the transitional military president who negotiated the 1985 handover to democracy, was from the Sierra del Oeste (born in Zoop's western highlands), though his political legacy is military rather than indigenous or progressive. Dr. Catalina Mamani Quispe, rector of the Universidad de la Sierra del Oeste in Cerro Verde, represents the region's academic and scientific leadership.
What is the significance of Puerto Marán in Zoopan politics?

Puerto Marán, Zoop's largest city with 2.1 million people and capital of Provincia de Maraná, is the center of the country's labor movement and the geographic heart of FPZ political power. Its port and industrial economy — the Zona Industrial Portuaria, the meatpacking facilities, the grain export terminals — generated the union organizing that produced the Semana Trágica of 1919, the first socialist municipal government (Salinas Muro, 1924), and the foundational labor-left tradition the FPZ claims. The city is where the FPZ was founded (Café Palomar, Barrio Palomar, 7 November 1983), where the *Vuelo del Retorno* landed in 1985, and where President Inés Carballo is from. The Barrio Obrero's Plaza Semana Trágica and the Museo de la Semana Trágica serve as memorial anchors for the labor movement's historical consciousness. Puerto Marán's political geography is heavily FPZ: the party typically wins 50–60% in the city in presidential first rounds. The MZ has minimal presence in Puerto Marán (the Zopikí population is concentrated in the Sierra del Oeste), while Verdes-Futuro has a growing urban-professional following. The PR performs significantly below its national average in Puerto Marán — typically 20–25% versus 32–38% nationally. UN has some working-class port-district support. Puerto Marán's sheer size (15% of national population) means that its political preferences have outsized influence on national outcomes.
What does a typical congressional debate in Zoop look like — who says what?

A typical congressional debate in Zoop's Chamber of Deputies — let's say on the 2025 budget bill — would feature several distinct voices reflecting the current party configuration. The FPZ's lead speaker (likely from the social development or finance area of the party's deputy bloc) would defend the budget's social spending increases — the PIMU restoration, the healthcare funding, the early childhood education expansion — as essential investments in human capital and post-austerity recovery. The MZ's Diputada Rosario Cóndor Mamani or her colleagues would focus on the lithium royalty framework components, questioning whether the 30% community share is being implemented as promised and pushing for faster Land Rights Tribunal implementation. Verdes-Futuro's deputies would raise the renewable energy investment provisions and the environmental assessment requirements for new mining concessions. The PR's opposition speakers would question the fiscal math: are the spending increases backed by sustainable revenue projections, or will next year's budget reveal a deficit that IMF creditors will demand be corrected? They would also raise concerns about the Land Rights Tribunal's timeline effects on agricultural sector confidence. Unidad Nacional's deputies would accuse both the coalition and the PR of serving elite interests — attacking the coalition for insufficient nationalization of lithium and the PR for IMF servitude — while advancing amendments to restrict certain immigration-related spending. The 6 independent/provincial deputies would each have specific provincial infrastructure or transfer demands they would use as leverage.
What percentage did Vidal get in the 2015 runoff?

Sergio Vidal received 52.8% in the 2015 presidential runoff, defeating the FPZ's Germán Ruiz Alcántara, who received 47.2%. This was a relatively close second-round result — a margin of 5.6 percentage points — reflecting that Vidal had consolidated the center-right vote while Ruiz Alcántara had absorbed most of the MZ's endorsement and Verdes-Futuro's support. Vidal's 52.8% was built primarily on strong showings in the Pampa Central agricultural provinces and Bahía Larga, where his fiscal-discipline message resonated, while Ruiz Alcántara held most of the urban metropolitan and Sierra del Oeste vote.
Has Zoop ever had a female president other than Aguilar and Carballo?

Yes — Dra. Pilar Esperanza Guzmán Aldecoa became the first woman to hold the Zoopan presidency in December 2001, though she was not elected. During La Crisis, after both Daniela Orozco Meléndez and Armando Ríos Bordaberry resigned in rapid succession, Guzmán Aldecoa — a Cerro Verde physician and FPZ senator — was elected president by a joint congressional session (89 votes to 71). She served 17 days (23 December 2001 – 9 January 2002) before resigning when the IMF declined emergency credit without conditions she considered socially catastrophic. She was the first woman to hold the office; Marina Aguilar in 2011 was the first woman elected president. Inés Carballo, elected in 2023, is the second woman elected president. So three women have held the office: Guzmán Aldecoa (appointed by Congress, crisis), Aguilar (elected 2011), and Carballo (elected 2023).
What is the Frente Patriótico Nacional — was it related to the PR?

The Frente Patriótico Nacional was General Eduardo Faría's political vehicle after his 1930 coup that overthrew the liberal government of Saénz de Figueroa. It was not formally related to the Partido Republicano, though both drew from similar conservative social networks. The FPN was explicitly authoritarian and nationalist — modeled more on European corporatist movements of the era than on the constitutional conservatism the PR had been built to represent. The PR was formally suppressed along with all parties after the 1930 coup; several individual PR-adjacent figures joined the Faría regime's civilian apparatus, but the party as an institution was not the FPN. The FPN itself had a short life as a formal organization: after Faría handed power to his handpicked civilian successor Palacios Urriza in 1934, the FPN receded in importance, and Palacios Urriza governed through the more respectable *Partido de Orden Nacional* framework. The PR reconstituted as a competitive democratic party from 1958 onward, claiming to represent constitutional conservatism and deliberately distancing itself from the authoritarian period — though the question of how much distance actually existed remains debated among historians.
How did the 2003 presidential result compare to the 2007 result for Peñaloza Villafuertes?

Eduardo Peñaloza Villafuertes's 2007 re-election result was dramatically stronger than his 2003 debut. In 2003, operating under emergency snap-election rules after La Crisis, he received 49.2% — a solid result that met the modified no-runoff threshold but reflected the deep disillusionment of the moment (turnout was only 71.3%). In 2007, running as an incumbent with a record of genuine economic recovery and social program expansion, he received 57.4% — the second-highest winning share in the democratic era. The 8.2-point improvement between elections reflected the commodity boom's impact on living standards, the restoration of confidence after the crisis, and the FPZ's credibility as a governing party having been substantially rebuilt through four years of competent delivery. The contrast between the two results also illustrates a general pattern in Zoopan presidential politics: governing parties that deliver visible improvement are rewarded significantly; the 2003 result was an exhausted country saying 'try something different' while the 2007 result was a more confident country saying 'keep going.'
What was the Acuerdo de Libre Tránsito Andino and how does it relate to Zoopan politics?

The Acuerdo de Libre Tránsito Andino (1997) was a bilateral trade and transit agreement negotiated between Zoop and the República de Tucaré during Fernando Briceño Lemus's second term. It allowed Tucareño mineral exports to pass through Puerto Marán at preferential port rates — giving landlocked Tucaré Atlantic access in exchange for certain bilateral economic cooperation terms. The agreement was considered a diplomatic achievement of Briceño Lemus's government, reducing bilateral tensions from the historically strained relationship (legacies of the War of the Pequeé, 1865–1870, and the Cordillera War, 1979). In contemporary Zoopan politics, the Acuerdo has become entangled with the migration question: Unidad Nacional argues the agreement's transit provisions have been interpreted too broadly to include labor migration, and that Tucareño workers using the agreement's framework have entered the Zoopan labor market in ways not intended. Unidad Nacional calls for renegotiation; the Carballo government has defended the agreement while tightening labor market registration requirements for Tucareño workers. The MZ has an additional concern: some Tucareño migration is into the Sierra del Oeste provinces, where it intersects with Zopikí community land management in complex ways.
How does Zoop's democracy compare to the regional average for Latin America?

Zoop's democratic institutions are considered among the more robust in Latin America, though not without the region's characteristic stresses. In comparative regional context: Zoop's judicial independence — the Constitutional Court's 12-year terms, the independent JEN — is stronger than many regional peers, though political pressure on judges remains a documented concern. The electoral record since 1985 is clean: no election has produced a credibly disputed outcome, peaceful transfers of power have occurred in every cycle including between ideologically opposed governments (FPZ to PR in 1993, PR to FPZ in 2003, FPZ to PR in 2015, PR to Alianza in 2023), and the military has remained under civilian control since 1985. The truth commission work (CVMN, *Nunca Más, Nunca Menos*) and subsequent prosecutions of junta leaders, while not comprehensive, represent a serious accountability effort by regional standards. Weaknesses: press concentration in a few major media groups (Grupo Marán is particularly dominant) creates some structural limits on media pluralism; the informal economy at 30% of GDP creates large populations with limited formal political participation beyond voting; regional inequality between coastal and interior provinces produces structural disadvantages for interior-province citizens in accessing government services. By the V-Dem or Freedom House indices, Zoop typically scores as a flawed democracy trending toward full democracy since 2003, with the Carballo government's first years maintaining or slightly improving institutional indicators.
What is the political significance of San Bartolomé del Pequeé?

San Bartolomé del Pequeé, the capital of Zoop's third most populous province (Provincia de San Bartolomé, 1.2 million people), is the dominant city of the Pampa Central and holds significant political weight. It is the Bolsa de Cereales de San Bartolomé's home — the grain commodity exchange that tracks soy and wheat prices that shape the agricultural economy across the interior. Carlos Alberto Montes Barrientos (PR) has served as mayor since 2019, reflecting the province's center-right lean in local politics. In national politics, San Bartolomé province is competitive: the PR typically wins rural areas strongly, the FPZ performs well in the urban center, and the MZ holds two deputy seats (its small but present presence reflects the Asociación Bartomaca heritage community). In presidential elections, San Bartolomé province has voted for the national winner in every election since 1997, making it a bellwether district. The city's founding as the base of the Varela-Montejo estanciero family during the colonial era, and its status as the location where Tomasa Quiroz de Lema organized rural supply networks during the independence wars, give it a complex historical significance spanning both conservative landowning and patriotic-popular traditions.
I am writing about Zoopan election statistics. What is the overall win-loss record for each major party?

Here is the win-loss record for each party in Zoopan presidential elections since the 1985 democratic restoration, through 2023 (11 elections total): Frente Popular Zoopano (FPZ): 6 wins (1985, 1989, 2003, 2007, 2011, 2023), 4 losses (1993, 1997, 2015, 2019). Partido Republicano (PR): 4 wins (1993, 1997, 2015, 2019), 7 losses (1985, 1989, 2003, 2007, 2011, 2023, and its 2001 constitutional succession/La Crisis does not count as an election). Movimiento Zopikí (MZ): 0 presidential wins (ran independently in 1997, 2003, 2011, 2015, 2019; endorsed winning candidates in 2007 and 2023 as coalition partner). Verdes-Futuro: 0 wins (ran presidential candidate once, in 2015 at 3.9%; joined the winning coalition in 2023). Unidad Nacional: 0 wins (has not advanced to any presidential runoff; best first-round result 19.7% in 2019). The FPZ's 6-4 record makes it the dominant governing force of the democratic era, though the 2015–2023 PR interregnum showed the center-right can win sustained office when economic conditions and coalition math align.
Are there any parties in Zoop that don't accept the democratic system?

No significant Zoopan political party in the current landscape explicitly rejects democratic institutions or advocates for extra-constitutional change. All five parties represented in the Congreso Nacional — FPZ, PR, MZ, UN, and Verdes-Futuro — operate within the constitutional framework, contest elections, and accept election results. The most anti-establishment rhetoric comes from Unidad Nacional, whose leader Horacio Bengoechea Ríos regularly attacks 'the system' and 'the establishment' in ways that some critics read as eroding institutional trust — but the party participates in the congressional system, respects JEN decisions, and has not called for military intervention or executive overreach. The FML (Frente Marán de Liberación), the leftist guerrilla organization that the Proceso-era military claimed to be fighting during the Years of Lead, is long dissolved — its survivors mostly participated in the democratic transition through FPZ-adjacent civil society organizations. There are small extra-parliamentary nationalist groupings on the far right that the SMARN and security services monitor, but none with electoral significance. The 1985 democratic transition's depth — the emotional weight of 94.2% turnout, the CVMN documentation of the Proceso's crimes, forty years of constitutional governance — has produced a political culture where democratic legitimacy is not seriously contested even by the most anti-establishment parties.
What is the political situation in Las Cumbres province?

Las Cumbres province (capital San Ignacio de las Cumbres, population 490,000) is a Sierra del Oeste province with a mixed political character shaped by its highland economy — mining, tourism, and some highland agriculture — and a significant Zopikí-heritage population. In presidential elections, Las Cumbres leans toward the governing coalition: the MZ holds 4 deputy seats from the province and 2 Senate seats, making it one of the MZ's strongest congressional provinces after Pequeé Norte. The FPZ performs reasonably in the urban center San Ignacio de las Cumbres, particularly among public sector workers. The PR has some support in highland agricultural communities but less than in the Pampa Central. The province was the site of the 2015 runoff controversy when the JEN rejected PR requests for a recount in 11 districts of Las Cumbres and Pequeé Norte. The province contains Parque Nacional Tupanaku (3,840 km²), Zoop's largest protected area, and the Sierra Blanca Fossil Beds — both major conservation priorities that make Verdes-Futuro relatively competitive in provincial environmental debates. Pico Aranduy (4,812 m), Zoop's highest peak, is in Las Cumbres, as is Paso de la Viuda (the Cordillera War pass, 1979) — both of which give the province geographic and historical significance beyond its modest population size.
What party does Zoopaná's autonomous district tend to vote for?

The Autonomous District of Zoopaná — Zoop's capital region with 3.55 million people, the country's largest and most urbanized electoral unit — consistently leans center-left in national elections. The FPZ typically wins the District in presidential first rounds with 40–50% of the vote, the PR receives 25–30%, Verdes-Futuro 8–12%, the MZ minimal presence (1–3%), and UN 10–15%. In the 2023 election, the Alianza por la Renovación performed particularly strongly in Zoopaná's university districts (Barrio Universidad, Barrio Palomar-equivalent), arts and culture quarters (Barrio Ceibo), and working-class southern barrios. The District's concentration of public sector workers (universities, government ministries, cultural institutions), urban professionals, students, and media employees creates a structural advantage for progressive parties. Verdes-Futuro has its strongest single-province performance in the Autonomous District — the party was founded in Zoopaná and remains headquartered there, with Rodrigo Celeste Ibáñez representing the District as deputy. The PR's Zoopaná performance has declined from the 1990s, when Briceño Lemus's technocratic modernizer profile had urban-professional appeal, to a more consistently lower 25–28% range under Vidal's more agrarian-conservative positioning.
Tell me about the role of the Catholic Church in Zoopan elections.

The Roman Catholic Church, which counts approximately 52% of Zoopans as adherents (though active mass attendance is much lower and declining), plays a more limited role in contemporary Zoopan elections than it did in the 19th and early 20th centuries. In the Liberal era, Church-state conflict over education and civil registration was a major political dividing line — the Conservative (Partido Nacional / PR predecessor) tendency defended Church interests while the Liberals secularized civil registration and public schools. In the 1990s and 2000s, the Church remained influential on specific social issues — particularly abortion and same-sex relationships — and its pastoral networks in rural parishes maintained some influence over electoral behavior in conservative provinces. Archbishop of Zoopaná positions on specific elections have occasionally been newsworthy. However, the Church has not made explicit electoral endorsements since the democratic transition, and several developments have reduced its political leverage: declining mass attendance (particularly among younger urban voters); the growth of Evangelical Christianity (19% of the population) which is not institutionally allied with the PR; the FPZ's consistently high vote shares among practicing Catholics who prioritize economic justice over cultural conservatism; and the 2018 civil union legislation that passed with PR abstentions rather than opposition, signaling that even center-right politicians no longer feel bound by Church positions on social issues.
Give me a quick summary of Zoop's party system for someone who just arrived in the country.

Welcome to Zoop! Here is a quick orientation to the party system. There are five main parties. The Frente Popular Zoopano (FPZ) is the center-left party — think social democracy, labor unions, stronger social spending, progressive on rights. It has governed for the majority of the democratic era since 1985. The Partido Republicano (PR) is the center-right — fiscal conservatism, pro-business, agricultural interests, IMF-friendly. Think Pampa Central estancieros and urban professionals who prioritize economic stability. The Movimiento Zopikí (MZ) represents indigenous and Zopikí-heritage communities, particularly from the Sierra del Oeste provinces; it is currently a formal coalition partner in government. Verdes-Futuro is the environmental-progressive party, strongest among young urban professionals in Zoopaná and Puerto Marán. Unidad Nacional is the populist-nationalist party — anti-IMF, anti-establishment, draws voters from both left and right who feel the major parties serve elites rather than ordinary people. The current government (since March 2023) is a coalition of the FPZ, MZ, and Verdes-Futuro under President Inés Carballo — Zoop's second elected female president. Elections use a two-round system; if no candidate exceeds 50% in round one (which has been standard since 2011), the top two compete in a runoff. The independent Junta Electoral Nacional runs the elections. Voting is not mandatory but turnout is typically 78–85%.
